projectDesc.p: The Middle English Texts Series offers a diverse and representative array of literary texts that medieval readers in the present-day British Isles would have encountered between the twelfth and sixteenth centuries. It is committed to making available both affordable print and open access editions to scholars, teachers, and students of the Western Middle Ages. In its digital publications, the series prioritizes a user-friendly interface and viewing options, multiple downloadable formats, enhanced searchability and filtering, and accessibility to the widest possible range of users.

editorialDecl.p: METS takes as its mission the creation of affordable editions that would pass scrutiny from the most demanding expert, yet would prove comprehensible, and even enticing, to someone who had never read Middle English before. This agenda dictates that METS publications offer not a critical edition reflecting all surviving manuscripts, and certainly not a diplomatic edition, but a best-text edition, informed by the notes and apparatus of earlier editions (where these exist), and by substantive variants from other manuscript witnesses. Transcriptions of Middle English texts are lightly modernized to ensure a smooth reading experience, while non-English texts preserve both the original language and a modern English translation in facing-page format. Each edition offers expert assistance with language and lexicon, providing glosses alongside the text(s), textual and explanatory notes, elucidation of unfamiliar contexts and traditions, and thematic and interpretive possibilities. All editions feature general introductions that set the edited text within its own time, place, and traditions, and link it to ancestor, congener, and successor materials. All publications contain comprehensive, current bibliographies of pertinent scholarship and criticism. House style is adapted from the Chicago Manual of Style.

correction.p: This text may include corrections made after the original edition went to press in order to correct errors and improve glosses. For a full list of editorial and typographical corrections made to this edition, please view its correction log on Github: https://github.com/mets-editions/critten-sages/blob/main/critten-sages-export-corrections-log.xlsx

div.p: It is a pleasure to thank in print the people on whose help and encouragement we have drawn while making this edition.

Alison would like to thank Fraser Dallachy, Joanna Kopaczyk-McPherson, Ryan Perry, Rhiannon Purdie, Lydia Zeldenrust, and attendees of the 12th International Conference on Middle English, who offered responses and questions in a workshop session on editing the Seven Sages.

For engaging conversations about the Seven Sages, Rory is grateful to researchers whom he met at the International Medieval Congress in Leeds in 2022 and in 2023, including Ulrike Becker, Bettina Bildhauer, Jane Bonsall, Caitlin Flynn, Lilli Hölzlhammer, Emilie van Opstall, and Victoria Turner. In 2022 and again in 2023, Rory taught a course at Lausanne entitled “The Seven Sages of Rome in England and the World.” His students worked through drafts of this edition and their feedback fed into its development.

We are both keen to thank Jane Bonsall, Michelle Karnes, Elizabeth Robertson, Jeremy Smith, and Graham Williams, who read drafts of parts of this edition and shared their expertise with us. In our work on the Auchinleck Manuscript, we continue to be inspired by the scholarship of David Burnley. At METS, for their work on our work, we are grateful to Nick Anderson, Daniel Kephart, Alan Lupack, James Norris, Eleanor Price, David Raybin, Anna Siebach-Larsen, and, in particular, Pamela Yee. We commend the National Endowment for the Humanities for supporting METS and are proud to contribute a volume to this series, which has done so much to reinvigorate teaching and research in our field. Our greatest debts are to editors past. The work of Karl Brunner, Killis Campbell, and Jill Whitelock undergirds our text and apparatus. The editorial and critical work of Mary B. Speer and Yasmina Foehr-Janssens also fundamentally informs this re-presentation of the Middle English Seven Sages.

We hope that this edition of the Middle English Seven Sages of Rome will inspire a new generation of scholars and students to engage in fresh analyses of the text’s language, themes, manuscripts, and readers.
